meaning: It’s time to get up / time to wake up now; a gentle prompt from an elder or caregiver to a child or junior.
usage: Used as a soft, everyday wake-up call, often spoken by a parent or older family member to children in the morning; typically comes at the very start of an interaction or scene to signal the transition from sleep to activity.
example: 妈妈轻轻推开门，说："该起床喽，今天要去郊游呢。"
verify_why: Natural colloquial Mandarin phrase meaning ‘time to get up now’; structure 该+V+喽 is common and idiomatic.

meaning: A casual greeting meaning “How are you?” or “What are you doing right now?”; here it also functions as a playful call sign among friends.
register: American English, informal urban speech among friends
usage: Used at the start of a phone call or encounter; can be repeated and exaggerated for comic effect or camaraderie.
example: He called his friend and just said, “What’s up?” to see if he wanted to hang out.
verify_why: Common colloquial English greeting meaning “how are you/what’s going on?”

expression: Nothin', just watching the game, having a bud.
meaning: A relaxed way of saying “I’m not doing anything special, just watching a sports game and drinking a Budweiser beer.”
usage: Answer to a casual “What’s up?” when you want to emphasize you’re just chilling; can be used as a stock phrase to signal low-key relaxation.
example: When she asked what he was up to, he said, “Nothin’, just watching the game, having a bud.”
verify_why: Natural conversational English response describing current activity; fits beer‑ad context (Budweiser).

meaning: An affirmation meaning “Yeah, that’s right” or “I feel you”; repeating it adds emphasis and rhythm.
usage: Used to agree with someone’s statement in a laid-back way; often follows a friend’s description or opinion.
example: “Man, it’s been a long week.” “True, true.”
verify_why: Colloquial affirmation in English meaning “that’s right / I agree,” often repeated for emphasis.
